name: Combretovium
text: Your train passes near the site of Combretovium, on the train's {side}, where two Roman forts, and perhaps a small settlement, stood by the crossing of the River Gipping on the road from London to Caistor St Edmund. Nothing is visible now, but finds there include a deliberately broken statuette of the emperor Nero.

name: Portman Road
text: Your train passes near Portman Road, on the train's {side}, home of Ipswich Town since 1884 and the largest football ground in East Anglia. Its biggest crowd, 38,010, came to see Ipswich play Leeds United in March 1975, and England played Croatia there in 2003.

name: St Mary at Stoke
text: Your train passes near St Mary at Stoke, on the train's {side}, a Grade I church on a site that has had a church since the 10th century. A small medieval church with a hammer-beam roof survives as the north aisle beside a large Victorian extension by William Butterfield, from 1872.

name: Ardleigh Reservoir
text: Your train passes near Ardleigh Reservoir, on the train's {side}, a 120-acre lake made in the valley of the Salary Brook after an Act of Parliament of 1969. It supplies drinking water to Anglian Water and Affinity Water, and is used for sailing and angling.

name: Iron Latch
text: Your train passes near Iron Latch, on the train's {side}, a small Essex Wildlife Trust reserve of grassland and ash woodland at Eight Ash Green. Nightingales nest in its trees and hedges, and common blue and purple hairstreak butterflies are found there.

name: St Andrew's Church, Marks Tey
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church, on the train's {side}, whose nave was built around 1100 of rubble, puddingstone and Roman bricks, perhaps from a Roman villa not yet found. The upper two thirds of its 16th-century tower are of timber.

name: St Mary the Virgin Church, Kelvedon
text: Your train passes the parish church of St Mary the Virgin, on the train's {side}, a Grade I church whose oldest part, at the north-west corner of the nave, was probably built early in the 12th century. Its aisles were added around 1230 and 1250.

name: Witham Town Hall
text: Your train passes near the town hall in Newland Street, on the train's {side}, which began in the 15th century as The George, a timber-framed coaching inn on the road from London to Colchester. It was encased in red brick around 1800, with three false windows hiding the old roof, and was later a bank.

name: Boreham
text: Your train passes near Boreham, on the train's {side}, whose name in the Domesday Book, Borham, is thought to mean "village on a hill". Henry VIII stayed at nearby New Hall, and in the 1930s the car maker Henry Ford bought Boreham House, where Ford tractor mechanics were trained.

name: New Street Works
text: Your train passes the New Street Works, on the train's {side}, built for the Marconi Company in 1912 and credited as the first purpose-built radio factory in the world. It took only 17 weeks from start to finish, and gave Chelmsford its claim to be the "home of the radio".

name: Chelmsford Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Chelmsford Cathedral, on the train's {side}, a parish church rebuilt in the 15th and 16th centuries that became a cathedral in 1914. Its south porch was extended in 1953 to mark Anglo-American friendship and the many American airmen stationed in Essex in the war.

name: Mountnessing Windmill
text: Your train passes near Mountnessing Windmill, on the train's {side}, a post mill of 1807 on a site with records of a windmill since 1477. It was repaired in 1937, the year of George VI's coronation, as a memorial to the king, and restored to full working order in 1983.

name: Brentwood Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Brentwood Cathedral, on the train's {side}, a Gothic parish church of 1861 enlarged between 1989 and 1991 by Quinlan Terry in an Italianate classical style, inspired by the early Italian Renaissance and Christopher Wren. The money for it came from donors who chose to stay anonymous.

name: The Golden Fleece, Brook Street
text: Your train passes near the Golden Fleece, on the train's {side}, an old inn at Brook Street, once a hamlet of South Weald and now part of Brentwood. Its original hammer-beam hall roof can still be seen in the dining room's entrance.

name: Hutton Country Park
text: Your train passes near Hutton Country Park, on the train's {side}, a 37-hectare nature reserve of grassland, oak and hornbeam woodland and ponds, with the River Wid along its northern edge. Large red damselflies and orange tip butterflies live there.

name: Norsey Wood
text: Your train passes near Norsey Wood, on the train's {side}, an ancient coppice woodland whose rides, some thought to date from the Iron Age, are described as the oldest known woodland rides to survive. It is the likely site of the Battle of Billericay in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

name: Rayleigh Castle
text: Your train passes near Rayleigh Castle, on the train's {side}, the earthworks of a motte-and-bailey castle built soon after the Norman Conquest by Swein, son of Robert FitzWimarc. It is one of 48 castles named in the Domesday Book, and the only one in Essex.

name: Shotgate Thickets
text: Your train passes Shotgate Thickets, on the train's {side}, an Essex Wildlife Trust reserve on the north bank of the River Crouch, with oak woodland, ponds and thorn thickets. Great crested newts and water voles live there, and more than 70 kinds of bird have been seen.

name: Woodham Fen
text: Your train passes Woodham Fen, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of saltmarsh and rough grassland between two tidal creeks running into the River Crouch. Reed buntings and yellow wagtails are found there, and common lizards and slowworms live in the grass.

name: South Woodham Ferrers
text: Your train passes South Woodham Ferrers, on the train's {side}, which was sparse farmland until the station opened in 1889 and grew into a town after a plan by Essex County Council in 1974. Many of its streets are named from Tolkien, such as Gandalf's Ride, Hobbiton Hill and Arwen Grove.

name: Blue House Farm
text: Your train passes near Blue House Farm, on the train's {side}, an Essex Wildlife Trust reserve and working farm on the north bank of the River Crouch. A field there is flooded each winter, and around 2,000 Brent geese come to feed.

name: Creeksea Place
text: Your train passes near Creeksea Place, on the train's {side}, a house built by Sir Arthur Harris in 1569, a date still moulded on an original lead rainwater head. Its walled garden and orchard were used in the BBC's adaptation of Great Expectations.

name: Goldsands Road Pit
text: Your train passes Goldsands Road Pit, on the train's {side}, a geological Site of Special Scientific Interest. It holds the earliest evidence of an ancient course of the combined Thames and Medway, which flowed north-east across Essex about 400,000 years ago.

name: Dutch Cottage
text: Your train passes near the Dutch Cottage, on the train's {side}, an octagonal thatched house named after the Dutch settlers who built many of south Essex's sea walls. The door says 1621, but experts think it was built around 1740; it is said that with no corners, evil spirits had nowhere to lurk.

name: Spa Pump Room, Hockley
text: Your train passes near the Spa Pump Room, on the train's {side}, built in 1842 after a retired couple from Cheltenham found their well water eased the wife's asthma. It closed as a pump room in the early 1850s and was later a Baptist chapel, a billiard hall and a clothing factory.

name: Rochford Hall
text: Your train passes near Rochford Hall, on the train's {side}, a Grade I manor that belonged to Thomas Boleyn, father of Anne Boleyn, and was the home of her sister Mary and Mary's second husband, William Stafford. It is now the clubhouse of a golf club.

name: Prittlewell royal Anglo-Saxon burial
text: Your train passes the site of the Prittlewell princely burial, on the train's {side}, found in 2003 during a survey before a road was widened. The burial dates from about 580 and is thought to be of Sæxa, brother of King Sæberht of Essex; gold foil crosses show he was an early Christian.

name: Southend Central Museum
text: Your train passes near Southend Central Museum, on the train's {side}, in the town's first free library, built in 1905 with money from Andrew Carnegie. It has a planetarium and, since 2019, a gallery of finds from the royal Saxon burial at Prittlewell.

name: Cressing Temple
text: Your train passes near Cressing Temple, on the train's {side}, given to the Knights Templar in 1136 by Queen Matilda, wife of King Stephen, and one of their earliest estates in England. Two Templar barns survive, one claimed to be the oldest standing timber-framed barn in the world.

name: Church of St Etheldreda, White Notley
text: Your train passes near the church of St Etheldreda, on the train's {side}, built mostly in the 10th century on the site of a Roman temple, with Roman brick and stone in its walls. A small medieval window shows St Etheldreda, set in a stone frame reused from an Anglo-Saxon grave marker.

name: Alec Hunter Academy
text: Your train passes near Alec Hunter Academy, on the train's {side}, a school opened in 1959 and named after the weaver and textile designer Alec Hunter. Keith Flint and Liam Howlett of The Prodigy were both pupils there.

name: Warner Textile Archive
text: Your train passes near the Warner Textile Archive, on the train's {side}, in part of the old mill of Warner & Sons, the Braintree silk and velvet makers who made the Queen's coronation robes. Its 100,000 items make it the second-largest public collection of textiles in the UK, after the V&A.

name: Chappel Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Chappel Viaduct, 1,060 feet long and 75 feet high across the Colne Valley, the longest bridge in East Anglia. Its 32 arches took more than six million bricks, made from clay dug at Bures, and it was finished in 1849.

name: East Anglian Railway Museum
text: Your train passes the East Anglian Railway Museum, on the train's {side}, which keeps railway buildings, engines and carriages in the station's old goods yard and buildings. Started in 1968, it was where the band Blur played their first concert, in 1989.

name: Gainsborough's House
text: Your train passes near Gainsborough's House, on the train's {side}, the birthplace in 1727 of the painter Thomas Gainsborough, youngest of nine children. Parts of the house date from around 1520, and it has been a museum and gallery since 1961.

name: Colchester power station
text: Your train passes near the site of Colchester power station, on the train's {side}, built on Hythe Quay by the town council. It supplied electricity to Colchester and the area around from 1900 until 1960.

name: Church of St Leonard at the Hythe
text: Your train passes near the church of St Leonard at the Hythe, on the train's {side}, for many years the church of the port of Colchester. Royalist soldiers sheltered in it during the siege of 1648, and bullet holes survive in its door.

name: Rowhedge Ironworks
text: Your train passes near the site of Rowhedge Ironworks, on the train's {side}, a shipyard on the River Colne that built some 900 vessels between 1904 and 1964. It specialised in small craft for buyers abroad, often sent in kit form, including boats for Lake Titicaca and the Nile.

name: Cockaynes Wood
text: Your train passes Cockaynes Wood, on the train's {side}, an ancient wood listed in the Domesday Book and now a nature reserve, with heathland, meadows and flooded old quarries. Barn owls and a rare weevil live there.

name: Frating Abbey
text: Your train passes near Frating Abbey, on the train's {side}, a 19th-century farmhouse on a site long said to be an abbey, though there is no evidence it was more than a priory's farm. The boundaries of two parishes and two parliamentary seats run through the house.
